title: Best AI video generators in 2026: Veo, Runway, Kling, Pika, HeyGen
excerpt: Sora is gone. We compare Google Veo and Omni, Runway, Kling, Pika, Synthesia and HeyGen on models, pricing as of 4 October 2026 and commercial-use terms.
content:
The best AI video generators in 2026 are Google's Gemini Omni and Veo 3.1, Runway Gen-4.5, Kling 3.0 (with Kling 4.0 rolling out now), and Pika for cinematic clips, plus Synthesia and HeyGen for presenter-style avatar videos. OpenAI's Sora, last year's headline act, is gone: the app closed in April 2026 and its API was switched off on 24 September. Here is what each costs as of 4 October 2026 and what its terms allow.

Key takeaways

  • Sora is discontinued. The app closed on 26 April 2026 and the API on 24 September.
  • Google has the broadest offer. Omni Flash comes with every paid Google AI plan, Veo 3.1 is sold by the second, and Google Vids is free.
  • Licensing differs more than quality. Pika and HeyGen keep commercial rights off their free plans. Kling's general terms bar commercial use of outputs without written permission. Runway and Synthesia don't claim ownership of what you make.

What happened to OpenAI Sora

OpenAI released Sora 2 alongside an invite-only iOS app called Sora on 30 September 2025, according to TechCrunch. It opened in the US and Canada. Its "cameos" feature let people verify themselves with a short recording, then let friends put that likeness into generated scenes.

The run was short. OpenAI said on 24 March 2026 that it was closing Sora, and TechCrunch reported that the company gave no reason. It reported downloads falling from 3.3 million in November to 1.1 million in February. The app and website closed on 26 April 2026, according to The Decoder. OpenAI's deprecations page says the Videos API and all Sora 2 models were removed on 24 September 2026, with no replacement.

Sora is here as a warning: if your work depends on one vendor's model, keep your prompts and source files and know where you would move. If you want to build these models rather than buy them, see roles at OpenAI and our AI and ML jobs board.

The cinematic generators, tool by tool

Google: Gemini Omni, Veo 3.1 and Flow

Google now has two video model families. The newer is Gemini Omni, announced at I/O on 20 May 2026 as a model that turns text, image, video or audio references into video, according to Google's I/O round-up. Omni Flash went to paid Google AI subscribers worldwide through the Gemini app and Flow, Google's AI filmmaking studio, and is free in YouTube Shorts Remix for adults. Google's Gemini API guide now makes Omni Flash the default, keeping Veo 3.1 for native audio, extension and first-and-last-frame control.

Veo 3.1 itself dates from 15 October 2025. According to the Google Developers Blog, it added richer audio, reference images and scene extension past a minute. Google added a cheaper Veo 3.1 Lite on Vertex AI, its cloud platform, on 4 April 2026, according to Google Cloud. Google's Veo page lists 1080p and 4K output.

Pricing as of 4 October 2026:

  • Consumer plans: Google's US plans page lists AI Plus at $4.99 a month with 200 Flow credits and Gemini Omni Flash. AI Pro is $19.99 with 1,000 Flow credits and a limited trial of Veo 3.1 Lite. AI Ultra starts at $99.99, with a $199.99 top tier, and comes with 10,000 or 25,000 credits and the highest Veo 3.1 access. In India the same tiers cost ₹399, ₹1,950, and ₹6,500 or ₹19,500 a month.
  • Developers: the Gemini API pricing page (updated 1 October 2026) charges per second of video. Veo 3.1 costs $0.40 at 720p or 1080p and $0.60 at 4K. Veo 3.1 Fast costs $0.10, $0.12 or $0.30, and Veo 3.1 Lite costs $0.05 or $0.08 with no 4K. Veo has no free API tier.
  • Free: since 23 September 2026, anyone with a personal Google or Workspace account can make 1080p clips in Google Vids with a Flash-Lite version of Gemini Omni 1.1, according to Android Authority.

Licensing and labels: Google's Terms of Service (effective 30 July 2026) say Google won't claim ownership of content you generate. Google still gets a licence to use it to run and improve services. Every Veo and Omni video carries SynthID, Google's invisible watermark. Google also added C2PA Content Credentials, an industry standard that records a file's origin and edits.

Runway Gen-4.5

Runway released Gen-4.5 on 1 December 2025. At launch it ranked first on the Artificial Analysis text-to-video benchmark with an Elo score of 1,247, according to Runway. Runway admits objects can still appear or vanish.

Pricing as of 4 October 2026, from Runway's pricing page: the Free plan gives 125 credits once. Standard is $15 a month, or $12 a month billed yearly, for 625 credits a month. Pro is $35 ($28 yearly) for 2,250 credits, and Max is $95 ($76 yearly) for 9,500 credits. Gen-4.5 uses 12 credits per second, so Standard covers about 52 seconds of Gen-4.5 video a month. Paid plans have no watermarks. They also include Kling 3.0 and other third-party models.

Licensing: Runway's terms of use (updated 15 September 2026) say it does not claim ownership of your inputs or outputs and does not restrict commercial use, as long as you follow the agreement. You do give Runway a perpetual, irrevocable licence to use inputs and outputs to train and improve its models.

Kling 3.0 and Kling 4.0

Kling belongs to Chinese short-video firm Kuaishou. Kling 3.0 launched on 5 February 2026 with Video 3.0, Video 3.0 Omni and two image models, according to Kuaishou's press release. It makes clips of up to 15 seconds with native audio in English, Chinese, Japanese, Korean and Spanish. Kuaishou said Kling had more than 60 million creators.

Kling 4.0 is next. According to Kling's blog, early access began on 28 September 2026 and the full model launches in October. It makes 3- to 30-second clips at up to 4K, with 10-bit HDR "coming soon". It accepts up to 10 keyframes. We could not read Kling's consumer prices, so check them in the app.

Licensing: read Kling's terms closely. Its terms of service (updated 21 April 2026) say you own the intellectual property in your content. They also say you may not use outputs for commercial purposes without Kling's written permission, and that outputs must be labelled as made with Kling AI. Kling has separate paid-service terms we could not retrieve, so confirm what your plan allows.

Pika

Pika is now a multi-model studio. Its homepage describes a rebuilt "new Pika" announced on 17 September 2026. It brings video, image and sound together and offers Pika 2.5 alongside third-party models such as Seedance 2.5 and Google's Omni Flash.

Pricing as of 4 October 2026, from Pika's pricing page: Free has no monthly credits (you buy packs). Starter is $10 a month ($8 yearly) for 900 credits. Creator is $35 ($28) for 3,150 credits, and Fancy runs $95 to $880 ($76 to $704) from 8,550 credits. All plans are watermark-free. Only Creator, Fancy and Enterprise include a commercial licence.

Licensing: Pika's terms (updated 4 August 2026) say you keep your outputs. Use is personal and non-commercial unless your plan expressly allows commercial use. Outside enterprise deals, Pika may train on anonymised or aggregated data.

Avatar tools: Synthesia and HeyGen

Synthesia and HeyGen put a lifelike presenter on screen to read your script, which suits training, sales and localised explainers.

Synthesia

Synthesia's pricing page lists a free Basic plan with 10 minutes of video a month and a Synthesia watermark. Starter is $29 a month billed monthly, with 1,250 credits (about 12 minutes of video) and no logo. Pro is $89 a month with 6,000 credits (about 60 minutes) and five personal avatars. Its customer terms (effective 20 July 2026) say customers own their output. Anyone whose likeness or voice becomes a custom avatar must be of legal age and give "free and informed consent". Synthesia's avatars page says personal avatars need a live on-camera consent check that cannot be uploaded or skipped.

HeyGen

HeyGen's pricing page lists a Free plan with three videos a month of up to one minute each, with access to its Avatar IV model. Creator is $29 a month with 600 credits, videos up to 30 minutes, 1080p export and no watermark. Pro is $49 with 1,000 credits and 4K export. Business is $149 a month plus $20 per seat. HeyGen's terms (updated 23 July 2026) assign ownership of output to users on paid plans. Free-plan users get only a revocable, non-commercial licence. The terms ban uploading images of people without their consent, and HeyGen's avatars page says custom avatars need verified consent from the person being recreated.

How to choose

  • You need short cinematic shots for ads or social: try Google's Gemini Omni Flash through an AI Plus or Pro plan, then compare it with Runway Gen-4.5. Runway also includes Kling 3.0.
  • You are building a product: the Gemini API has clear per-second rates, from $0.05 a second for Veo 3.1 Lite at 720p. Sora's API ended on six months' notice, so design for swapping models.
  • You need talking-head training or sales videos: choose Synthesia or HeyGen. HeyGen's $49 Pro plan adds 4K export; Synthesia's Pro plan gives about an hour of video a month.
  • You are on a zero budget: Google Vids is free; HeyGen's free plan and Pika's free and Starter plans exclude commercial use.
  • You do client work: confirm commercial rights and save a copy of the terms on the day you publish.

We track releases on our launches page and in news.

Risks: deepfakes, consent and copyright

Likeness and deepfakes. Sora showed how fast realistic faces get misused: TechCrunch reported unauthorised deepfakes of Martin Luther King Jr. and Robin Williams on the app. Never upload someone's face or voice without their written permission.

Disclosure rules. Article 50 of the EU AI Act requires providers of systems that generate synthetic audio, image or video to mark outputs in a machine-readable way. Anyone publishing a deepfake must disclose it. ArtificialIntelligenceAct.eu lists 2 August 2026 as the application date.

Copyright in your output. Owning an output under a vendor's terms is not the same as holding copyright in it. On 29 January 2025 the US Copyright Office concluded that prompts alone do not make someone the author of an AI output. Protection needs enough human expressive input. Where rights matter, confirm with a qualified IP lawyer.

Training on your work. Runway, Kling and Pika (outside enterprise deals) all take licences to use what you upload and generate to improve their models. Don't put confidential footage into consumer plans.

Bottom line

In 2026, staying power, licence terms and consent matter as much as clip quality. Google offers the widest range of entry points, Runway the most flexible workspace, and Kling the longest clips once 4.0 ships, though its commercial terms need checking. For presenter videos, Synthesia and HeyGen are the safer choice.

FAQ

Is OpenAI Sora still available?

No. The Sora app and website closed on 26 April 2026, and OpenAI removed the Sora 2 models and Videos API from its API on 24 September 2026.

Which AI video generator is free?

Google Vids makes free 1080p clips for personal Google accounts. Runway, Synthesia and HeyGen have limited free tiers.

Can I use AI-generated videos commercially?

It depends on the tool and plan. Runway doesn't restrict commercial use, and HeyGen and Pika allow it only on qualifying paid plans. Kling's general terms require written permission. Check the current terms before you publish.

Can I make an AI avatar of someone else?

Only with their consent. Synthesia requires a live on-camera consent check, and HeyGen requires verified consent from the person being recreated.
